title: Corpus-Supported Distractors: Auditing Retrieval-Augmented Quiz Generation Against the Stem
content: A multiple-choice item whose wrong option is also a correct answer to its own stem is not a hard item, it is a broken one, and every faithfulness metric a retrieval-augmented quiz generator currently ships will score that option as clean. The reason is structural. Groundedness is a two-place relation between an option and the retrieved passage, item validity is a three-place relation among stem, option and passage, and no deployed metric supplies the third argument. We name the failure a corpus-supported distractor, build a stem-conditioned detector for it, and run that detector inside a ten-arm design on a 13,461-passage science-exam corpus standing in for course material, with three seeds and 100 items per arm per seed. Grounded generation leaves the corpus supporting a wrong option on 3.24% of distractor slots, against 0.68% for a generator denied the passage, and 1.00% of slots (9 of 894, Wilson 95% CI [0.34%, 1.79%]) survive the further test that the option stays supported under a narrowed stem, against 0.11% (1 of 885) for the ungrounded arm. Three seeds cannot certify that gap (paired t(2) = -1.84, p = 0.21) and a replication on a second corpus does not reproduce it at all. Four grounding-based faithfulness filters each raise the conditional rate to between 1.34% and 2.01%, which looks like the filter making the defect worse until a retention-matched random-drop null reaches 1.79% by discarding items at random. Counted rather than divided, the three entailment-family filters left the flagged-slot count at 9 while discarding half the pool, and they are indistinguishable from the attrition null on the counts themselves (Fisher exact p = 1.00). The rate rose because the denominator halved. We report the arithmetic, the pool size at which the statistical question becomes answerable, and a circularity that no pool size fixes, namely that a filter selecting on entailment cannot be scored by an endpoint that reads the same entailment signal.
